## Where we are

This morning you fit Bayesian models in the FANGS app. This afternoon we fit the same kind of model by writing the code ourselves in R with [Nimble](https://r-nimble.org). We build up to the summative challenge in small steps:

1. Read the data and look at coral cover.
2. Fit a Poisson GLM to site totals.
3. Add site random effects and fit the full transect data.
4. Fix poor mixing with a non-centred parameterisation.
5. Check the model and make publication-quality plots.
6. Add an observation-level random effect to deal with overdispersion.

**The scenario.** In Kia Province, Solomon Islands, divers ran three transects on each reef and recorded the per-cent cover of branching *Acropora*. This coral is the nursery habitat for juvenile bumphead parrotfish. Logging washes sediment onto reefs, so we expect cover to be lower closer to logging.

> **Data.** Hamilton, R.J., Almany, G.R., Brown, C.J., Pita, J., Peterson, N.A. & Choat, J.H. (2017) Logging degrades nursery habitat for an iconic coral reef fish. *Biological Conservation* 210: 273–280. <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.biocon.2017.04.025>. Lightly modified for teaching.


## Bayesian software options for R users

FANGS is for learning. For research you will want one of the established engines. The choice is mostly a trade-off between how much code you write and how much control you get.

| Package | Computational speed | Code complexity | Flexibility | Installation requirements | Use in ecology |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Stan** (`rstan`, `cmdstanr`) | Fast for continuous parameters; gradient-based HMC/NUTS scales well to many parameters | High — you write the full model in Stan's own C++-like language, with declared blocks and types | Very high, but no discrete parameters (they must be marginalised out) | Needs a working C++ toolchain; models compile before running (slow first run) | Widespread, and the standard in the quantitative ecology literature |
| **brms** | Same engine as Stan, so same sampling speed, plus compile time per model | Low — one-line `lmer`-style formulas, e.g. `cover ~ dist_to_logging_km + (1 \| site)` | Moderate-high: huge range of built-in families and terms, but hard to go outside them | As Stan (it generates and compiles Stan code for you) | Very widespread; now the default first choice for most applied ecologists |
| **INLA** | Very fast — approximates the posterior instead of sampling, often seconds where MCMC takes minutes | Low-moderate — formula interface, but priors and spatial terms use their own idiom | Restricted to latent Gaussian models (covers GLMMs, spatial and temporal models) | Not on CRAN; installed from the R-INLA repository with bundled binaries | Common in spatial ecology and species distribution modelling; less so elsewhere |
| **JAGS** (`rjags`, `R2jags`) | Slowest of these for large or hierarchical models; Gibbs/slice sampling, pure interpreter | Moderate — BUGS language, close to how you'd write the model on paper (this is FANGS' syntax) | High; handles discrete parameters, which Stan cannot | Needs the JAGS program installed separately from R, then the R package | Historically the workhorse and still very common in older papers and textbooks |
| **Nimble** | Faster than JAGS — compiles models to C++; usually slower than Stan for big continuous models | Moderate — BUGS language like JAGS, plus some R boilerplate to build and compile the model | Highest — you can write your own distributions and samplers in R-like code | CRAN package, but needs a C++ toolchain to compile models | Growing steadily, especially in population ecology and capture-recapture work |

A rough rule: use **brms** for anything that fits a standard formula, **INLA** when you have spatial data and need speed, and **Nimble** or **Stan** when the model is unusual enough that you need to write it out yourself. We use Nimble this afternoon because its model code is the same BUGS language you already used in FANGS, so the step up from the app is a short one. Its also easy to install from CRAN.

```{r}
#| label: packages
library(tidyverse)
library(nimble)
library(coda)
library(MCMCvis)

library(ggdist)
```


## 1. Read and explore the data

We read the data straight from the course website.

```{r}
#| label: read-data
url <- "https://www.seascapemodels.org/FANGS/course/data/random-effects.csv"
dat <- read_csv(url)
glimpse(dat)
```

Each row is one transect. There are 20 sites and 3 transects per site.

### Why a Poisson?

```{r}
#| label: cover-summary
summary(dat$cover)
mean(dat$cover < 20)   # proportion of transects below 20% cover

ggplot(dat, aes(x = cover)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2, fill = fangs[["accent"]]) +
  labs(x = "Branching Acropora cover (%)", y = "Number of transects")
```

Cover is a per cent, so strictly it can't go above 100 and a binomial would be the textbook choice. But when the counts are small relative to the maximum, the binomial and Poisson are nearly identical. Our transects average about 11% cover, well below 100, so the upper bound almost never matters and a Poisson is a reasonable approximation.

A few transects reach 40–50%, where the approximation is weaker.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Extension
Fit a binomial model with a size of 100 and compare the results with the Poisson.
:::

### Site totals

For our first model we ignore the transects and work with one value per site. We **sum** the three transects rather than averaging them. Nimble's Poisson only accepts whole numbers, and a sum of counts is still a count.

```{r}
#| label: site-totals
site_dat <- dat |>
  group_by(site, dist_to_logging_km) |>
  summarise(cover = sum(cover), .groups = "drop")

site_dat
```

## 2. A Poisson GLM on site totals

### The model

We keep this first model as simple as possible: an intercept and a single slope for distance to logging. It is the same structure you would write as a one-predictor linear model in R, but with a log link and a Poisson likelihood.

```{r}
summary(glm(cover ~ dist_to_logging_km, data = site_dat, family = poisson))
```

```{r}
#| label: glm-code
glm_code <- nimbleCode({
  beta0 ~ dnorm(0, sd = 2)   # intercept:     log cover at average distance
  beta1 ~ dnorm(0, sd = 1)   # distance slope

  for (i in 1:N) {
    log(mu[i]) <- beta0 + beta1 * dist[i]
    cover[i] ~ dpois(mu[i])
    y_rep[i] ~ dpois(mu[i])   # replicate data for the posterior predictive check
  }
})
```

Step by step:

1. **`nimbleCode()`** holds the model description. It looks like R, but Nimble reads it as a model definition, much like the model text in FANGS.
2. **The two priors** are the regression coefficients. The `~` means "is distributed as".
3. **The loop runs over the 20 sites.** The `<-` is a fixed calculation, not a random draw.
4. **`log(mu[i])` is the log link.** The expected count is the exponential of the linear predictor, so it is always positive.
5. **`cover[i] ~ dpois(mu[i])`** says the observed total cover follows a Poisson distribution with mean `mu[i]`.
6. **`y_rep[i]`** has the same distribution as `cover[i]`, but we don't give it any data. On each iteration Nimble simulates it from the Poisson, using that iteration's `mu[i]`. This gives draws from the posterior predictive distribution, which we use for the posterior predictive check. It's the same as the "generated quantities" idea you may have seen in Stan.

::: {.callout-note}
## Reading the coefficients
Both coefficients live on the log scale, so each has a plain multiplicative meaning:

| Coefficient | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `beta0` | log total cover for a site at the average distance from logging |
| `beta1` | change in log cover per one SD of distance (about 5 km) |

Exponentiating turns them into things you can picture: `exp(beta0)` is the expected site total at average distance, and `exp(beta1)` is the multiplicative change in cover per SD of distance. A `beta1` above zero means cover rises as you move away from logging, which is the direction the sediment story predicts.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## A note on `dnorm` in Nimble
In FANGS, `dnorm(0, 2)` means a normal distribution with mean 0 and standard deviation 2. Nimble follows the older BUGS convention, where the second number is the *precision*, which is 1 / variance. So `dnorm(0, 2)` in Nimble means an SD of about 0.71, a much tighter prior than you intended.

Always name the argument: `dnorm(0, sd = 2)`. Then your priors mean the same thing they meant in FANGS this morning.

```{r}
#| label: precision-demo
1 / sqrt(2)   # the SD you would get from dnorm(0, 2) in Nimble
```
:::

### Data and constants

Nimble separates **data**, which are things the model has a likelihood for, from **constants**, which are fixed inputs such as indices, sample sizes and covariates.

We standardise distance. Distance goes up to about 20 km, so on the raw scale a slope prior with SD 1 would allow effects as large as $e^{20}$ across the gradient. After standardising, `beta` is the effect per SD of distance, which is about 5 km, and our priors become sensible.

```{r}
#| label: glm-data
consts <- list(
  N    = nrow(site_dat),
  dist = as.numeric(scale(site_dat$dist_to_logging_km))
)
data <- list(cover = site_dat$cover)
```

Here `N` and `dist` are constants, and the observed site totals are the only data node.

### Prior predictive check

The model block is a recipe for generating data. If we run it forwards with no data, Nimble draws the parameters from their priors, then calculates `mu`, then simulates `cover`. That's the prior predictive distribution.

```{r}
#| label: glm-prior-pred
# A copy of the model with no data, so Nimble can simulate every node
prior_model <- nimbleModel(glm_code, constants = consts)
c_prior     <- compileNimble(prior_model)

# 1000 simulated data sets: one row per draw, one column per site
sim_cover <- t(replicate(1000, {
  c_prior$simulate()   # draw the betas from the priors, then mu, then cover
  c_prior$cover
}))

summary(as.vector(sim_cover))
mean(sim_cover > 300)   # proportion of impossible values

tibble(cover = as.vector(sim_cover)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = cover + 1)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = fangs[["cyan"]]) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 301, linetype = "dashed", colour = fangs[["orange"]]) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Simulated site total cover + 1 (log scale)", y = "Count")
```

A few things to note about the code:

- **We build a separate model object without data.** `simulate()` skips data nodes by default, so on a model with data, `cover` would never change. A copy with no data also leaves the model we fit later untouched.
- **`c_prior$simulate()` and `c_prior$cover`** use `$` to call a method and read a value from the model object. This is how you work with Nimble models from R.
- **`t()` transposes the result.** `replicate()` returns one column per draw, and we want one row per draw, the same layout as `y_rep` later.

Three transects of up to 100% cover means a site total can't go above 300, and the largest observed total is 137. Most prior draws should sit below 300, while still allowing a wide range of plausible values.

### Fitting the model

Fitting in Nimble takes a few more steps than pressing *Run* in FANGS, because Nimble compiles the model and the sampler to C++.

```{r}
#| label: glm-fit
# Build and compile the model
glm_model <- nimbleModel(glm_code, constants = consts, data = data,
                         inits = list(beta0 = 0, beta1 = 0))
c_model <- compileNimble(glm_model)

# Set up, build and compile the sampler
mcmc_conf <- configureMCMC(glm_model,
                           monitors = c("beta0", "beta1", "y_rep"))
glm_mcmc  <- buildMCMC(mcmc_conf)
c_mcmc    <- compileNimble(glm_mcmc, project = glm_model)

# Run: 4 chains, 2000 burn-in, 4000 kept samples per chain
samples <- runMCMC(c_mcmc,
                   nchains = 4,
                   niter   = 6000,
                   nburnin = 2000,
                   samplesAsCodaMCMC = TRUE)
```

::: {.callout-note}
In Nimble, `niter` **includes** the burn-in. To keep 4000 samples after a 2000-iteration burn-in, set `niter = 6000`.
:::

`nimbleMCMC()` wraps all of these steps into one call. It's handy once you know what each step does.

::: {.callout-note}
## Predictions inside the model
Print `mcmc_conf` and you'll see that Nimble has given the `y_rep` nodes `posterior_predictive` samplers. These simply simulate new values each iteration and don't change the parameter estimates. Two trade-offs:

- Every monitored prediction adds a column to the output. Use `params` or `pars` in summaries and plots so they only show the parameters you want.
- To change what you predict, for example a new prediction grid, you need to rebuild and recompile the model.
- If you want you can assemble predictions after the model fitting by just taking samples and applying the model formula to those. This gives more flexibility but increases the risk of mistakes if you change the model definition but then forget to change the prediction calculation. 
:::

### Summary, R-hat and ESS

```{r}
#| label: glm-summary
MCMCsummary(samples, params = c("beta0", "beta1"), round = 2)
```

There is one row per parameter, with the posterior mean, SD and quantiles, then `Rhat` and `n.eff` (the effective sample size). We want R-hat at about 1.00 and n.eff in the hundreds or more.

### Trace plots

```{r}
#| label: glm-trace
mcmc_trace(samples, pars = c("beta0", "beta1"))
mcmc_dens_overlay(samples, pars = c("beta0", "beta1"))
```

Each parameter gets a panel with the four chains in different colours. If the chains have mixed well, the four density curves sit almost on top of each other.

### Posterior predictive check

The `ppc_` functions in bayesplot are the posterior predictive plots the brms community use. They need the observed data and a matrix of simulated data sets, with one row per posterior draw. Nimble has already simulated these as `y_rep`, so we just pull out those columns.

```{r}
#| label: glm-ppc
# Stack all chains into one matrix of draws
post <- as.matrix(samples)

# One row per draw, one column per site, in site order
y_rep <- post[, paste0("y_rep[", 1:consts$N, "]")]

ppc_dens_overlay(site_dat$cover, y_rep[1:100, ])
ppc_rootogram(site_dat$cover, y_rep)
```

The site totals vary far more than a Poisson allows. Some sites have zero cover and others well over 100. The observed data sit outside most of the simulated data sets, so the model is **overdispersed**. Reefs differ for many reasons that distance alone doesn't capture. That is what random effects are for.

## 3. Adding site random effects

Now we use the full transect data. Each site gets its own random intercept, and a hyperparameter controls how far apart those intercepts can spread.

```{r}
#| label: re-code
re_code <- nimbleCode({
  # Fixed effects
  beta0 ~ dnorm(0, sd = 2)   # intercept:     log cover at average distance
  beta1 ~ dnorm(0, sd = 1)   # distance slope

  # Hyperparameter: SD of site effects
  sigma_b ~ dexp(1.54)

  # Site random effects
  for (s in 1:Nsite) {
    b[s] ~ dnorm(0, sd = sigma_b)
  }

  # Likelihood, one row per transect
  for (i in 1:N) {
    log(mu[i]) <- beta0 + beta1 * dist[i] + b[site[i]]
    cover[i] ~ dpois(mu[i])
  }
})

re_consts <- list(
  N     = nrow(dat),
  Nsite = n_distinct(dat$site),
  site  = as.integer(factor(dat$site)),
  dist  = as.numeric(scale(dat$dist_to_logging_km))
)
re_data <- list(cover = dat$cover)
```

What is new compared with the GLM:

1. **The site effects `b[s]`.** There is one per site, all drawn from a normal distribution centred on zero. The mean is zero because `beta0` already holds the average. If `b` had its own mean as well, the model couldn't tell that mean apart from `beta0`. That's the over-specification issue covered in Module 20 of the FANGS course.
2. **The hyperparameter `sigma_b`.** This is the SD of the site effects: how different the reefs are from each other. It is estimated from the data, which is what makes the model hierarchical. Sites borrow strength from one another, and when `sigma_b` is small, each site's mean is shrunk more strongly towards the average.
3. **The prior on `sigma_b`.** It must be positive, so we use an exponential prior. This puts the most weight near zero, so unless the data say otherwise, it pulls the model towards "the reefs aren't very different". See the aside below for how we chose the rate of 1.54.
4. **Avoid vague priors on SDs.** A very wide prior such as `dunif(0, 100)` might feel safe, but on the log scale it allows reefs to differ by absurd factors. You may see such priors in older literature (`gamma(0.001, 0.001)` on the precision was also a common vague prior that is now widely regarded as problematic). With only 20 sites, the data can't rule those values out, and the variance parameter mixes badly.
5. **The `site[i]` indexing** is how each transect picks out the effect of its own reef. Writing 20 dummy variables by hand would be unbearable, which is exactly why random effects use indexing instead.
6. **Distance is scaled on the transect data.** Every site has three transects, so this gives the same scaling as scaling the site totals.

::: {.callout-note}
## Aside: choosing the rate of an exponential prior
Following McElreath (*Statistical Rethinking*, 2nd edition, 2020), we use an exponential prior for the site SD. To pick its rate, work backwards from something you can picture.

1. **Choose a multiple.** How different could a typical reef's cover be from the average reef? Say that a reef with about 7 times more (or less) cover than average would be surprising.
2. **Choose a probability.** Allow only a 5% chance that reef differences are bigger than that.
3. **Convert the multiple to the log scale.** The model works on log cover, so a multiple of 7 is an SD of $\log(7) \approx 1.95$.
4. **Solve for the rate.** For an exponential distribution, $P(\sigma_b > s) = e^{-\lambda s}$. Setting that equal to 0.05 gives

$$\lambda = \frac{-\log(0.05)}{\log(7)}$$

```{r}
#| label: exp-rate
multiple <- 7      # reef-to-reef multiple we'd find surprising
p_exceed <- 0.05   # probability the SD is larger than that

s_max <- log(multiple)
rate  <- -log(p_exceed) / s_max
rate

# Check it worked should = p_exceed
1 - pexp(s_max, rate)
```

That gives a rate of about 1.54, so the model line is `sigma_b ~ dexp(1.54)`.

Try other numbers. If you think a multiple of 20 is plausible, the rate drops to 1. A larger rate pulls harder towards zero.
:::

### Prior predictive check

The same three lines work for the hierarchical model. We just swap in the new code and constants. `simulate()` now also draws `sigma_b`, then a site effect for each reef, before simulating cover for every transect.

```{r}
#| label: re-prior-pred
re_prior   <- nimbleModel(re_code, constants = re_consts)
c_re_prior <- compileNimble(re_prior)

re_sim_cover <- t(replicate(1000, {
  c_re_prior$simulate()
  c_re_prior$cover
}))

summary(as.vector(re_sim_cover))
mean(re_sim_cover > 100)   # proportion of impossible transect values

tibble(cover = as.vector(re_sim_cover)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = cover + 1)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = fangs[["cyan"]]) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 101, linetype = "dashed", colour = fangs[["orange"]]) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Simulated transect cover + 1 (log scale)", y = "Count")
```

Each transect's cover can't go above 100%. The site effects add an extra layer of variation, so expect a longer right tail than for the GLM. If a large share of draws are above 100, go back to the aside and choose a smaller reef-to-reef multiple, which gives a tighter prior on `sigma_b`.

The centred and non-centred versions have the same priors, so this one check covers both.

### Fitting the centred model

The steps are the same as for the GLM. We add `sigma_b` and `b` to the inits and monitors.

```{r}
#| label: re-fit
re_model <- nimbleModel(re_code, constants = re_consts, data = re_data,
                        inits = list(beta0 = 0, beta1 = 0,
                                     sigma_b = 1, b = rep(0, re_consts$Nsite)))
c_re_model <- compileNimble(re_model)

re_conf   <- configureMCMC(re_model,
                           monitors = c("beta0", "beta1", "sigma_b", "b"))
re_mcmc   <- buildMCMC(re_conf)
c_re_mcmc <- compileNimble(re_mcmc, project = re_model)

re_samples <- runMCMC(c_re_mcmc, nchains = 4, niter = 6000, nburnin = 2000,
                      samplesAsCodaMCMC = TRUE)
```

### Checks

```{r}
#| label: re-checks
MCMCsummary(re_samples, params = c("beta0", "beta1", "sigma_b"), round = 2)

mcmc_trace(re_samples, pars = c("sigma_b", "beta0", "beta1"))

# The funnel: a site effect against log(sigma_b)
mcmc_scatter(re_samples, pars = c("b[1]", "sigma_b"),
             transformations = list(sigma_b = "log"))
```

What to look for:

- **`sigma_b` is the parameter to watch.** In the summary, look for an R-hat above 1.01 or an n.eff much lower than the others.
- **The scatter plot shows why.** When `sigma_b` is small, the site effects are squeezed close to zero. When it is large, they can spread out. This makes a funnel shape, and the sampler gets stuck in the narrow neck.
- **The intercept can mix badly too**, because `beta0` and the site effects trade off against each other.

## 4. The non-centred parameterisation

The non-centred parameterisation is a common trick to improve sampling for random effects models. 

```{r}
#| label: re-nc-code
re_nc_code <- nimbleCode({
  beta0 ~ dnorm(0, sd = 2)
  beta1 ~ dnorm(0, sd = 1)
  sigma_b ~ dexp(1.54)

  for (s in 1:Nsite) {
    z[s] ~ dnorm(0, sd = 1)       # standardised site effect
    b[s] <- sigma_b * z[s]        # rescaled to the real site effect
  }

  for (i in 1:N) {
    log(mu[i]) <- beta0 + beta1 * dist[i] + b[site[i]]
    cover[i] ~ dpois(mu[i])
    y_rep[i] ~ dpois(mu[i])       # replicate data for the PPC
  }

  # --- Generated quantities -------------------------------------------
  # Predicted cover for a typical reef (b = 0) along the distance gradient
  for (k in 1:Npred) {
    log(mu_pred[k]) <- beta0 + beta1 * dist_pred[k]
  }

  # Effect as a multiplier
  mult_dist <- exp(beta1 * d5)    # multiplicative change in cover per 5 km
})
```

Apart from the generated quantities at the end, the model hasn't changed, only the way it's written. Instead of drawing site effects directly from a distribution whose width depends on `sigma_b`, we draw standard normal values `z` and multiply them by `sigma_b`. The sampler now explores `z` and `sigma_b` separately, and the funnel disappears.

The generated quantities are all deterministic (`<-`) or have no data, so they don't affect the fit:

- **`mu_pred`** is the expected cover along a grid of distances. We'll plot it as the prediction curve.
- **`mult_dist`** is the distance effect as a multiplier per 5 km. `d5` converts 5 km into standardised distance units.

Calculating these inside the model is worth the effort. Both are non-linear functions of the coefficients, and doing the calculation on each draw propagates the uncertainty correctly — exponentiating a posterior mean is not the same as the mean of the exponentials.

The prediction grid has to be passed in as constants, so we build it before the model. We predict over the range of distances actually sampled.

```{r}
#| label: pred-grid
dist_mean <- mean(dat$dist_to_logging_km)
dist_sd   <- sd(dat$dist_to_logging_km)

pred_grid <- tibble(
  dist_km = seq(min(dat$dist_to_logging_km), max(dat$dist_to_logging_km),
                length.out = 50)
) |>
  mutate(k      = row_number(),
         dist_z = (dist_km - dist_mean) / dist_sd)

re_nc_consts <- c(re_consts, list(
  Npred     = nrow(pred_grid),
  dist_pred = pred_grid$dist_z,
  d5        = 5 / dist_sd
))
```

```{r}
#| label: re-nc-fit
re_nc_model <- nimbleModel(re_nc_code, constants = re_nc_consts, data = re_data,
                           inits = list(beta0 = 0, beta1 = 0,
                                        sigma_b = 1, z = rep(0, re_consts$Nsite)))
c_re_nc_model <- compileNimble(re_nc_model)

re_nc_conf   <- configureMCMC(re_nc_model,
                              monitors = c("beta0", "beta1", "sigma_b", "b",
                                           "y_rep", "mu_pred", "mult_dist"))
re_nc_mcmc   <- buildMCMC(re_nc_conf)
c_re_nc_mcmc <- compileNimble(re_nc_mcmc, project = re_nc_model)

re_nc_samples <- runMCMC(c_re_nc_mcmc, nchains = 4, niter = 6000, nburnin = 2000,
                         samplesAsCodaMCMC = TRUE)
```

`b` is now calculated from `z` and `sigma_b`, but we can still monitor and plot it.

### Checks, again

```{r}
#| label: re-nc-checks
MCMCsummary(re_nc_samples, params = c("beta0", "beta1", "sigma_b"), round = 2)

mcmc_trace(re_nc_samples, pars = c("sigma_b", "beta0", "beta1"))

mcmc_scatter(re_nc_samples, pars = c("b[1]", "sigma_b"),
             transformations = list(sigma_b = "log"))
```

Compare these with the centred model. R-hat and n.eff for `sigma_b` should improve, and the funnel should be gone.

## 5. Checking and interpreting the random effects model

### Posterior predictive check

```{r}
#| label: re-ppc
post_re  <- as.matrix(re_nc_samples)
y_rep_re <- post_re[, paste0("y_rep[", 1:re_consts$N, "]")]

ppc_dens_overlay(dat$cover, y_rep_re[1:100, ])
ppc_rootogram(dat$cover, y_rep_re)

# Does the model reproduce the number of zeros?
prop_zero <- function(y) mean(y == 0)
ppc_stat(dat$cover, y_rep_re, stat = "prop_zero")
```

Look closely at the zeros check. 26 of the 60 transects have zero cover. If the model predicts far fewer, the transects within a site still vary more than a Poisson allows. Site 8, for example, has transects of 7, 18 and 1. We come back to this in section 6.

A plot that's easier for readers to interpret shows each observed transect against its predictive interval:

```{r}
#| label: re-ppc-intervals
ppc_intervals(dat$cover, y_rep_re, x = dat$dist_to_logging_km) +
  labs(x = "Distance to logging (km)", y = "Cover (%)")
```

### Parameter estimates

```{r}
#| label: re-estimates
# Fixed effects and site SD
mcmc_areas(re_nc_samples, pars = c("beta0", "beta1", "sigma_b"), prob = 0.9)

# Distance effect as a multiplier per 5 km
mcmc_intervals(re_nc_samples, pars = "mult_dist")

# Site effects: which reefs are above or below average?
mcmc_intervals(re_nc_samples, regex_pars = "^b\\[")
```

How to read these:

- **The multiplier** is the multiplicative effect from Modules 14 and 15. A value of 1.5 means cover is 50% higher for every 5 km further from logging. If the interval crosses 1, the direction is uncertain.
- **`beta1` on the log scale** is the same information, which is why its density and the multiplier tell the same story in different units. Report the multiplier: readers can picture it.
- **Site effects** show shrinkage. Sites with all-zero transects are pulled towards the mean instead of going to minus infinity.

### Joint posteriors

```{r}
#| label: re-pairs
#| fig-height: 7
mcmc_pairs(re_nc_samples, pars = c("beta0", "beta1", "sigma_b"))
```

Things to discuss:

- **Intercept against slope.** Because we centred distance, `beta0` and `beta1` should be close to uncorrelated. That is the main practical reason to standardise a predictor: it decouples the intercept from the slope and the sampler explores the posterior more easily.
- **`sigma_b` against the intercept.** A sloping or curved shape shows that the overall level and the spread between reefs are partly confounded.
- **Centred vs non-centred.** Run the same pairs plot on `re_samples` to see the funnel next to the clean non-centred version.

### Publication-quality plots

The multiplier and the predictions were calculated inside the model, so we just need to get them out of the chains. `tidybayes` does this tidily. `gather_draws()` stacks the named quantities into long format, and `spread_draws()` splits indexed nodes like `mu_pred[k]` into a value column and an index column.

```{r}
#| label: effects-draws
effects <- re_nc_samples |>
  gather_draws(mult_dist) |>
  mutate(effect = "Distance to logging (per 5 km)")
```

**The effect as a multiplier:**

```{r}
#| label: effects-eye
ggplot(effects, aes(x = .value, y = effect)) +
  stat_halfeye(.width = c(0.66, 0.95), fill = fangs[["accent"]],
               colour = fangs[["text"]], slab_alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = fangs[["orange"]]) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Multiplicative effect on coral cover", y = NULL)
```

- The x-axis is on a log scale, so doubling (2) and halving (0.5) sit the same distance from 1.
- The thick bar is the 66% interval and the thin bar is the 95% interval.
- If the distribution sits clearly above 1, cover rises with distance from logging, which is the direction the sediment story predicts.

**Predicted cover along the distance gradient:**

```{r}
#| label: pred-plot
# 1000 draws is plenty for smooth ribbons
pred <- re_nc_samples |>
  spread_draws(mu_pred[k], ndraws = 1000) |>
  left_join(pred_grid, by = "k")

ggplot(pred, aes(x = dist_km, y = mu_pred)) +
  stat_lineribbon(.width = c(0.5, 0.8, 0.95), colour = fangs[["text"]]) +
  geom_point(data = dat, aes(x = dist_to_logging_km, y = cover),
             colour = fangs[["cyan"]], alpha = 0.6, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(fangs[["border"]], fangs[["muted"]],
                               fangs[["accent"]])) +
  labs(x = "Distance to logging (km)", y = "Branching Acropora cover (%)",
       fill = "Credible interval")
```

- **The line stops where the data stop.** The grid runs over the sampled range of distances only. Drawing the curve past the furthest site would be pure extrapolation, so the sampling design limits what we can conclude.
- **The curve is for a typical reef**, with the site effect set to zero. Because of the log link, this is the *median* reef. The mean across reefs is higher by a factor of $e^{\sigma_b^2/2}$.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Extension
Predict for an unsampled reef. Add `b_new ~ dnorm(0, sd = sigma_b)` to the model block, along with a second prediction, `log(mu_new[k]) <- beta0 + beta1 * dist_pred[k] + b_new`. Monitor `mu_new` and plot it in the same way. The ribbon will be much wider, because it includes the variation between reefs.
:::

## 6. An observation-level random effect

The zeros check showed that transects within a site still vary more than a Poisson allows. The fix uses the idea you have just learned: give every transect its own small random effect.

```{r}
#| label: olre-code
olre_code <- nimbleCode({
  beta0 ~ dnorm(0, sd = 2)
  beta1 ~ dnorm(0, sd = 1)
  sigma_b ~ dexp(1.54)   # reef-to-reef SD
  sigma_e ~ dexp(1.54)   # transect-to-transect SD

  for (s in 1:Nsite) {
    z[s] ~ dnorm(0, sd = 1)
    b[s] <- sigma_b * z[s]
  }

  for (i in 1:N) {
    e_z[i] ~ dnorm(0, sd = 1)
    log(mu[i]) <- beta0 + beta1 * dist[i] + b[site[i]] + sigma_e * e_z[i]
    cover[i] ~ dpois(mu[i])

    # Replicate data: a NEW transect on the same reef
    e_new[i] ~ dnorm(0, sd = 1)
    log(mu_rep[i]) <- beta0 + beta1 * dist[i] + b[site[i]] + sigma_e * e_new[i]
    y_rep[i] ~ dpois(mu_rep[i])
  }

  mult_dist <- exp(beta1 * d5)   # distance effect per 5 km
})
```

1. **`e_z[i]` gives each transect its own multiplier.** This turns the Poisson into a Poisson-lognormal distribution, which allows extra spread and extra zeros. It is non-centred from the start, for the same reason as the site effects.
2. **There are now two variance components.** `sigma_b` is how much reefs differ from each other. `sigma_e` is how much transects on the same reef differ. Comparing them is ecologically meaningful: is most of the variation in coral cover between reefs or within them?
3. **The prior on `sigma_e`** uses the same "multiple of 7, 5% chance" reasoning. Redo the aside's calculation with your own belief about how much transects on one reef can differ.
4. **Expect harder sampling.** The model now has 60 extra parameters. Check the n.eff for `sigma_e` especially, and be ready to increase `niter`.
5. **The replicates use new transect effects, `e_new`.** See the warning in the posterior predictive check below for why.

```{r}
#| label: olre-fit
olre_model <- nimbleModel(olre_code, constants = re_nc_consts, data = re_data,
                          inits = list(beta0 = 0, beta1 = 0,
                                       sigma_b = 1, z = rep(0, re_consts$Nsite),
                                       sigma_e = 1, e_z = rep(0, re_consts$N)))
c_olre_model <- compileNimble(olre_model)

# Don't monitor e_z or e_new: we never look at them directly
olre_conf   <- configureMCMC(olre_model,
                             monitors = c("beta0", "beta1", "sigma_b", "sigma_e",
                                          "b", "y_rep", "mult_dist"))
olre_mcmc   <- buildMCMC(olre_conf)
c_olre_mcmc <- compileNimble(olre_mcmc, project = olre_model)

olre_samples <- runMCMC(c_olre_mcmc, nchains = 4, niter = 6000, nburnin = 2000,
                        samplesAsCodaMCMC = TRUE)

MCMCsummary(olre_samples,
            params = c("beta0", "beta1", "sigma_b", "sigma_e"),
            round = 2)
mcmc_trace(olre_samples, pars = c("sigma_b", "sigma_e"))
```

### Posterior predictive check

::: {.callout-warning}
## A trap
If the replicates used the *fitted* transect effects, `y_rep[i] ~ dpois(mu[i])`, every transect would already have its own effect. The model would then reproduce the observations almost perfectly and the check would tell you nothing. So in the model block we draw a **new** transect effect, `e_new[i]`, for each replicate. That asks a fairer question: what would another transect on this reef look like?
:::

```{r}
#| label: olre-ppc
post_ol  <- as.matrix(olre_samples)
y_rep_ol <- post_ol[, paste0("y_rep[", 1:re_consts$N, "]")]

ppc_stat(dat$cover, y_rep_ol, stat = "prop_zero")
ppc_rootogram(dat$cover, y_rep_ol)
```

### Comparing the two models

```{r}
#| label: model-compare
bind_rows(
  tibble(model = "Site RE only",       mult = post_re[, "mult_dist"]),
  tibble(model = "Site + transect RE", mult = post_ol[, "mult_dist"])
) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = mult, y = model)) +
  stat_halfeye(.width = c(0.66, 0.95), fill = fangs[["accent"]],
               colour = fangs[["text"]], slab_alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = fangs[["orange"]]) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Distance effect (multiplier per 5 km)", y = NULL)
```

The interval should be wider in the second model. If you ignore overdispersion, you're overconfident about the effects you care about.

## Wrapping up

Back to the question: does coral cover rise with distance from logging, as the sediment-damage story predicts? Use the final model's distance multiplier to answer it, and keep in mind that the answer only holds over the range of distances the divers actually sampled.

A negative binomial likelihood is another common way to handle overdispersion, and it gives similar answers here. We used the observation-level random effect because it extends an idea you already know: adding one more level of variation to the model.

## References

Hamilton, R.J., Almany, G.R., Brown, C.J., Pita, J., Peterson, N.A. & Choat, J.H. (2017) Logging degrades nursery habitat for an iconic coral reef fish. *Biological Conservation* 210: 273–280.

McElreath, R. (2020) *Statistical Rethinking: A Bayesian Course with Examples in R and Stan*. 2nd edition. CRC Press.
